learn.hook: When you donate blood at a camp, the bag looks red, but more than half of it is a straw-coloured liquid called plasma.
points: All cells need a supply of nutrients and O₂ and removal of wastes, so organisms have circulating fluids. Simple organisms such as sponges and coelenterates circulate water from their surroundings through body cavities. Blood and lymph are the most common body fluids in higher animals.
Blood is a special connective tissue made of a fluid matrix (plasma) and formed elements.

Plasma is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid forming nearly 55% of blood. It is 90 to 92% water; proteins make up 6 to 8%. It also has minerals (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, HCO₃⁻, Cl⁻) and glucose, amino acids and lipids in transit.
Main plasma proteins: fibrinogen (clotting), globulins (defence mechanisms) and albumins (osmotic balance). Clotting factors are present in inactive form.
Serum is plasma without the clotting factors.

example.q: A blood sample is 5 L. About how much of it is plasma?
steps: Plasma is nearly 55% of blood.

learn.reallife: Blood banks in India separate donated blood into components; plasma is used to treat burns, shock and clotting disorders.

topics.title: Formed elements: RBCs, WBCs and platelets

learn.hook: During dengue season in India, doctors anxiously watch one number on the blood report: the platelet count.
points: Formed elements (RBCs, WBCs and platelets) make up nearly 45% of blood. RBCs are the most abundant: 5 to 5.5 million per mm³ in a healthy adult man. They are formed in red bone marrow in adults, lack a nucleus in most mammals and are biconcave.

RBCs contain haemoglobin, a red, iron-containing protein; a healthy person has 12 to 16 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL of blood. RBCs live about 120 days and are destroyed in the spleen (graveyard of RBCs).

WBCs (leucocytes) are colourless, nucleated, short-lived, 6000 to 8000 per mm³. Granulocytes: neutrophils (60 to 65%, most abundant, phagocytic), eosinophils (2 to 3%, resist infections, allergic reactions), basophils (0.5 to 1%, least, secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin; inflammation).
Agranulocytes: lymphocytes (20 to 25%, B and T types, immune responses) and monocytes (6 to 8%, phagocytic).

Platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments from megakaryocytes in bone marrow, 1,50,000 to 3,50,000 per mm³. They release substances involved in clotting; a fall in their number causes clotting disorders and excessive blood loss.

example.q: A WBC count is 8000 per mm³. About how many of these are neutrophils if they form 60%?
steps: Neutrophils = 60% of 8000.

topics.title: Blood groups: ABO, Rh and erythroblastosis foetalis

learn.hook: In an emergency, an O-negative donor's blood can save almost anyone. But mixing the wrong groups can be fatal. Blood groups decide.
points: ABO grouping is based on two surface antigens (A and B) on RBCs and two natural antibodies (anti-A, anti-B) in plasma.

Group A: antigen A, anti-B; can receive A, O. Group B: antigen B, anti-A; can receive B, O. Group AB: antigens A and B, no antibodies; can receive AB, A, B, O. Group O: no antigens, anti-A and anti-B; can receive only O.
Group O individuals are universal donors; group AB individuals are universal recipients.

The Rh antigen (similar to one in Rhesus monkeys) is present on RBCs of nearly 80% of humans (Rh+ve); those without it are Rh-ve. An Rh-ve person exposed to Rh+ve blood forms antibodies, so Rh should also be matched before transfusion.

Erythroblastosis foetalis: an Rh-ve mother with an Rh+ve foetus may be exposed to foetal blood during the first delivery and make anti-Rh antibodies. In later pregnancies these can leak into the Rh+ve foetus and destroy its RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice or even death. It is prevented by giving the mother anti-Rh antibodies immediately after the first delivery.

example.q: A person of blood group B needs blood. Which groups can safely donate?
steps: Group B has antigen B and anti-A antibodies.
Donor RBCs must not carry antigen A.
So donors of group B and O are safe.

learn.hook: Scrape your elbow in a game of kabaddi and within minutes a dark scab forms. That's a cascade of enzymes building a net of fibrin threads.
points: Coagulation (clotting) in response to injury prevents excessive blood loss. A clot (coagulum) is mainly a network of fibrin threads in which dead and damaged formed elements are trapped.

Fibrin is formed from inactive fibrinogen by the enzyme thrombin; thrombin is formed from inactive prothrombin by the enzyme complex thrombokinase, produced by a cascade of linked enzyme reactions involving plasma factors.
Injury stimulates platelets to release factors that activate coagulation; factors released by injured tissues can also start it. Calcium ions play a very important role.

As blood passes through tissue capillaries, water and small soluble substances move into spaces between cells, leaving larger proteins and most formed elements in the vessels. This interstitial (tissue) fluid has the same mineral distribution as plasma and is the medium of exchange between blood and cells.

The lymphatic system collects this fluid and drains it into major veins; the fluid inside it is lymph: colourless, containing lymphocytes for immunity, carrying nutrients and hormones, and absorbing fats through lacteals in intestinal villi. Unlike blood, lymph lacks RBCs and has fewer proteins.

example.q: Write the clotting cascade in order from injury to clot.
steps: Injury: platelets and tissues release factors.
A cascade forms thrombokinase.
Thrombokinase converts prothrombin to thrombin (Ca²⁺ needed).
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, whose threads trap cells to form a clot.
example.answer: Injury → thrombokinase → prothrombin to thrombin → fibrinogen to fibrin → clot

topics.title: Circulatory pathways and evolution of the vertebrate heart

learn.hook: A fish heart sends blood on one loop; your heart runs two separate loops at once. Evolution kept adding chambers.
points: Open circulatory system (arthropods, molluscs): blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces or body cavities called sinuses.
Closed circulatory system (annelids, chordates): blood always circulates through a closed network of vessels; flow can be regulated more precisely, so it is more advantageous.
Fishes: 2-chambered heart (one atrium, one ventricle); the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills, oxygenated blood goes to the body and returns: single circulation.

Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles): 3-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle). The left atrium gets oxygenated blood and the right atrium deoxygenated blood, but they mix in the single ventricle: incomplete double circulation.
Crocodiles, birds and mammals: 4-chambered heart (two atria, two ventricles); oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept separate: double circulation.

steps: Blood passes through the heart twice (from body and from lungs/skin).

example.answer: Because the two kinds of blood mix in the single ventricle.

topics.title: The human heart: structure, valves and nodal tissue

learn.hook: Your heart has its own built-in electrician, the SA node, which fires about 72 times a minute without any instruction from the brain.
points: The human circulatory (blood vascular) system has a muscular chambered heart, a closed network of branching blood vessels, and blood.

The heart is mesodermal, lies in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, slightly tilted to the left, about the size of a clenched fist. It is protected by a double-walled pericardium with pericardial fluid. It has two small upper atria and two larger lower ventricles; ventricle walls are much thicker than atrial walls.

A thin inter-atrial septum separates the atria; a thick inter-ventricular septum separates the ventricles; a thick fibrous atrio-ventricular septum separates atrium and ventricle of each side, with openings between them.

Valves: tricuspid valve (three cusps) between right atrium and right ventricle; bicuspid (mitral) valve between left atrium and left ventricle; semilunar valves at the openings of the pulmonary artery and aorta. Valves allow one-way flow and prevent backflow.

Nodal tissue: the sino-atrial node (SAN) in the right upper corner of the right atrium; the atrio-ventricular node (AVN) in the lower left corner of the right atrium near the AV septum; the AV bundle passes through the septa and divides into right and left bundles giving Purkinje fibres (the bundles with Purkinje fibres form the bundle of His). Nodal tissue is autoexcitable. The SAN generates the most action potentials (70 to 75 per minute) and is the pacemaker.

example.q: Trace the impulse from the pacemaker to the ventricular muscles.
steps: SAN (pacemaker) fires and the atria contract.
The impulse reaches the AVN.
It travels through the AV bundle, right and left bundles and Purkinje fibres.
The ventricular muscles contract.
example.answer: SAN → AVN → AV bundle → right and left bundles → Purkinje fibres → ventricles

Don't call the AVN the pacemaker

topics.title: The cardiac cycle, cardiac output and heart sounds

learn.hook: 'Lub-dub, lub-dub': each beat your doctor hears through a stethoscope is the sound of heart valves snapping shut.
points: Joint diastole: all four chambers relaxed; tricuspid and bicuspid valves open; blood flows from the pulmonary veins and vena cava through the atria into the ventricles; semilunar valves closed.
Atrial systole: the SAN fires, both atria contract, increasing ventricular filling by about 30%. The impulse passes via the AVN, AV bundle and bundle of His to the ventricles.

Ventricular systole (atria relax): ventricular pressure rises, closing the tricuspid and bicuspid valves; further rise opens the semilunar valves and blood flows into the pulmonary artery and aorta. Ventricular diastole: pressure falls, semilunar valves close; AV valves open as atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure; joint diastole again.

At 72 beats per minute, one cardiac cycle lasts about 0.8 s. Each ventricle pumps about 70 mL per beat (stroke volume). Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate, about 5000 mL (5 L) per minute; it is much higher in athletes.
First heart sound (lub): closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves. Second heart sound (dub): closure of semilunar valves. These sounds have clinical diagnostic significance.

example.q: Calculate cardiac output for a stroke volume of 70 mL and a heart rate of 72 beats per minute.
steps: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
70 × 72 = 5040 mL per minute.
That is about 5 L per minute.

learn.reallife: Cardiologists at Indian hospitals use a stethoscope to listen for abnormal 'murmurs' between lub and dub, which can signal faulty valves, such as after rheumatic heart disease.

revise.summary: The cardiac cycle runs joint diastole → atrial systole (adds about 30% filling) → ventricular systole (AV valves close, semilunar valves open) → ventricular diastole. Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate ≈ 5 L/min. Lub is AV valve closure; dub is semilunar valve closure.

traps: Don't divide stroke volume by heart rate for cardiac output

learn.hook: An ECG strip in an emergency ward is a story in waves: P, QRS and T tell a doctor exactly what the heart's electrical system is doing.
points: An electrocardiograph records the electrical activity of the heart during the cardiac cycle as an ECG. A standard ECG uses three leads: one to each wrist and one to the left ankle; more chest leads give detail.

P wave: electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, leading to atrial contraction. QRS complex: depolarisation of the ventricles, initiating ventricular contraction; contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of systole. T wave: return of ventricles to normal (repolarisation); the end of T marks the end of systole.

Counting QRS complexes in a given time gives the heart rate. Since ECGs have roughly the same shape for a given lead setup, deviations indicate possible abnormality, so the ECG has great clinical significance.

Pulmonary circulation: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium. Systemic circulation: left ventricle → aorta → arteries, arterioles, capillaries → tissues → venules, veins, vena cava → right atrium.

The hepatic portal system carries blood from the intestine to the liver through the hepatic portal vein before it enters systemic circulation. The coronary system circulates blood to and from the heart muscle.

example.q: An ECG strip shows 18 QRS complexes in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate?
steps: Each QRS complex is one heartbeat.
Heart rate = 72 beats per minute.

learn.reallife: Portable ECG machines are now used in rural health centres under India's health programmes to catch heart attacks early.

revise.summary: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity: P wave (atrial depolarisation), QRS complex (ventricular depolarisation) and T wave (ventricular repolarisation); counting QRS complexes gives heart rate. Double circulation has pulmonary and systemic circuits.

Standard ECG leads and heart rate from ECG

topics.title: Regulation of the heart and circulatory disorders

learn.hook: India has one of the world's largest numbers of people with high blood pressure, and many don't know it. A simple BP check can save lives.
points: The heart is myogenic: its activity is auto-regulated by nodal tissue. A neural centre in the medulla oblongata moderates it through the autonomic nervous system: sympathetic signals increase heart rate, strength of ventricular contraction and cardiac output; parasympathetic signals decrease heart rate, conduction speed and cardiac output. Adrenal medullary hormones also increase cardiac output.

Hypertension: blood pressure higher than normal (120/80 mm Hg; 120 is systolic or pumping pressure, 80 is diastolic or resting pressure). Repeated readings of 140/90 or higher indicate hypertension, which leads to heart disease and affects the brain and kidneys.

Coronary artery disease (atherosclerosis): deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue narrow the lumen of arteries supplying the heart muscle. Angina (angina pectoris): acute chest pain when not enough O₂ reaches the heart muscle; more common in middle-aged and elderly people.

Heart failure: the heart cannot pump blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs; also called congestive heart failure because lung congestion is a main symptom. It is not the same as cardiac arrest (heart stops beating) or heart attack (heart muscle suddenly damaged by inadequate blood supply).

Quick recap for exams: ABO compatibility depends on antigens and antibodies; the SAN is the pacemaker; open circulation uses sinuses while closed uses vessels; ECG waves P, QRS and T reflect atrial and ventricular electrical events.

example.q: A person's BP readings over three visits are 142/92, 145/94 and 140/90. Interpret.
steps: Normal BP is 120/80 mm Hg.
Repeated readings of 140/90 or higher indicate hypertension.
All three are at or above 140/90.

learn.reallife: The India Hypertension Control Initiative screens adults at primary health centres, because uncontrolled BP damages the heart, brain and kidneys.
